newsitem.title: UK: Britain issues election bomb threat guidelines.
newsitem.headline: Britain issues election bomb threat guidelines.

text.p: Britain on Friday issued guidelines for election officials on how to respond to any attempt by guerrillas to disrupt its May 1 poll as bomb attacks and security warnings again caused traffic chaos in England.

Returning officers, in charge of running the election in each of Britain's constituencies, were told to agree a security plan with police. This could include advance searches of polling venues and even searches of some voters' bags, officials said.

The advice was issued as bombs on a major motorway in central England and a suspicious device in Luton airport snarled Britain's transport system for the third time since last Friday. Irish guerrillas, fighting British rule of Northern Ireland, are believed to be behind the disruption.
Britain's Home Office (interior ministry) said the security guidelines had been issued in response to requests from election officials rather than as a direct result of Friday's travel chaos.

"We have no reason to believe there will be an attack on the poll or the count," a spokesman said. "The reason we issued the guidelines was in response to a number of requests from returning officers about what to do if there is disruption."

The guidelines said police would aim to "enable the electoral process to continue uninterrupted unless that would pose a clear risk to public safety". Voting could even be adjourned to the following day if disruption to the election was severe, the document said.

"Provided that an adequate security plan, based on police advice, has been put in place, it should be possible to avoid major disruption, such as evacuation of the premises, in almost all circumstances," it said.
"Should a bomb threat be received, the police will assess its credibility and consider, in the light of the security measures in place, what level of response is appropriate."
It warned that the counting of votes after polling ended could also be disrupted by bomb warnings.

Security sources say disruption of Britain's transport network is part of the Irish Republican Army's current strategy, aimed at winning concessions from Britain and maxiumum publicity with minimum loss of life.

The guerrillas want Britain to allow them into peace talks on the future of Northern Ireland, but Britain says they will be kept out of the talks until they call another ceasefire. A previous 17-month ceasefire ended in 1996.
